Today's Featured Research Reports

Shares of NVIDIA have underperformed the Zacks Semiconductor - General industry over the past year (-31.1% vs. -25.8%). Nevertheless, the company continues to benefit from broad demand for accelerated computing as customers build AI factories across hyperscalers, AI clouds, enterprises and sovereign buyers. Blackwell Ultra supports growth while Vera Rubin expands the platform across GPUs, CPUs, networking and software. 

Broader adoption, more content per system and usage-linked opportunities extend the growth runway, while cash generation supports substantial capital returns. The buildout also increases exposure to long-term supply commitments, extended customer payment terms and contingent guarantees. 

China remains constrained by export controls, while concentrated customer relationships, a costlier product ramp and competition can weigh on margins and cash flow. The founder's departure adds succession risk as NVIDIA moves to scale its next generation of systems.

(You can read the full research report on NVIDIA here >>>)

Cisco's shares have outperformed the Zacks Computer - Networking industry over the past year (+21% vs. +20.5%). The company's outlook benefits from a broad networking upgrade cycle, rising hyperscaler AI spending and deeper silicon and optics integration. New design wins and a large campus refresh opportunity support sustained demand. 

Security adoption and AI-led operations broaden the growth base, while tighter cost control adds operating leverage. Cash generation continues to fund shareholder returns. However, the shift toward hardware and higher memory costs are weighing on gross margins. Services growth remains modest, while competitive product cycles require disciplined execution. 

Acquisitions add integration exposure, and the stock's premium valuation leaves limited room for setbacks. The breadth of networking demand, rising AI revenue expectations and earnings leverage outweigh these risks, supporting the Outperform recommendation.

(You can read the full research report on Cisco here >>>)

Shares of BHP have outperformed the Zacks Mining - Miscellaneous industry over the past year (+32.3% vs. -0.1%). The company's low-cost iron ore franchise, growing copper earnings contribution and copper and potash projects support its long-term cash generation. Technology and the BHP Operating System continue to lift productivity, while fiscal 2026 cash flow and capital recycling provide funding flexibility. 

Record iron ore volumes and premium steelmaking coal exposure reinforce these strengths. Lower copper grades and processing variability constrain output before expansion projects contribute. Higher unit-cost guidance, heavy investment and Jansen capital escalation increase execution demands. 

Softer iron ore pricing and a less favorable Chinese pig iron outlook limit earnings visibility. Suspended nickel assets and Samarco's continuing cash obligations add portfolio and financial risks as BHP advances its organic growth program.

(You can read the full research report on BHP here >>>)

GEE's shares have underperformed the Zacks Staffing Firms industry over the past year (-6.3% vs. +47%). This microcap company with a market capitalization of $19.30 million is witnessing its contract staffing remains under pressure amid cautious hiring and labor-market uncertainty, while Hornet Staffing's failure to meet acquisition performance thresholds raises execution concerns. Cash generation also remains uneven. The shares trade near their historical median valuation. 

Nevertheless, GEE Group's return to profitability despite lower revenues reflects benefits from a richer direct-hire mix, cost reductions and productivity initiatives. Higher-margin direct-hire placements and improved contract staffing margins have strengthened overall profitability, while a leaner expense base could provide operating leverage when hiring demand recovers. 

Technology investments, including AI-enabled recruiting and integrated operating platforms, may further improve efficiency and scalability. The exit from industrial staffing has also sharpened the company's focus on professional staffing and higher-margin opportunities. 

(You can read the full research report on GEE here >>>)

Shares of Tandy Leather Factory have outperformed the Zacks Retail - Apparel and Shoes industry over the past year (+10% vs. +1.1%). This microcap company with a market capitalization of $18.02 million has seen third-quarter 2026 sales rose 7.3% to $18.5 million, while operating income rebounded to $0.6 million from a year-earlier loss. Pricing initiatives, sales campaigns and better product allocation support profitability. 

Tandy Leather Factory's 102-store network, specialist service, e-commerce reach and commercial offerings provide growth avenues, while a new loyalty program may encourage repeat purchases. A renewed $5 million buyback authorization adds flexibility, with no credit-facility borrowings reported. 

However, tariff refunds drove much of the quarterly margin gain, while a prior-year distribution shutdown eased comparisons. Cash fell to $5.7 million, inventory reached $37.5 million and nine-month operating cash outflow totaled $2.8 million. Higher occupancy costs and tariff uncertainty temper the improved outlook.

title: Own Dell Stock? Its Profit Isn't All Cash

Own Dell Stock? Its Profit Isn't All Cash
Trefis Team

HPE
IBM

Today's big story: Reported SEC Probe: Could Nvidia Stock Fall To $92?

Update, Nov 23: Dell rose about 23% in Monday morning trading, to about $341, after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and the Nasdaq 100 fund (QQQ) rose about 7%. This article's figures are at Friday's close. A higher price lifts both multiples equally, so Dell is still cheaper on profit than on cash.

Dell Technologies (DELL) closed at $278.02 on Friday, Nov 20. That was a fall of 11.0% in one day. Dell is still up 120.9% this year, price only. But it now sits 52.7% below its closing high of $588.40 on Sep 17.

So is Dell cheaper on profit or on cash? It is cheaper on profit. Dell trades at 15.9 times its net income over the four quarters to July. Free cash flow is the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment. On that measure, Dell trades at 21.2 times. The cash multiple is 32.9% higher than the profit multiple.

Why does Dell look more expensive on cash than on profit?

Only part of Dell's profit has arrived as cash. Over the four quarters to July, Dell turned 75.2% of its net income into free cash flow. That was $8.6 billion of cash against $11.4 billion of profit.

The latest quarter was thinner still. In the three months to Jul 31, 2026, free cash flow was 23.9% of net income. That is the lowest share since the quarter to Jan 31, 2025. In that quarter, free cash flow was below zero.

Dell turned only 23.9% of its July-quarter profit into cash, and its shares sit 52.7% below their September high. If Dell is a big part of your savings, that is a deep drop to sit through while you wait for the cash to show up. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record.

Where did Dell's cash go?

Money owed by customers is called receivables. In the six months to July, rising receivables used $11.8 billion of Dell's operating cash. Rising inventory used another $10.9 billion. Together they took $22.8 billion.

Suppliers filled much of that hole. Dell owed its suppliers more, and that added $16.2 billion to operating cash. Even so, operating cash flow over the six months was $6.3 billion. Net income over the same six months was $7.6 billion.

Dell's chief financial officer tied one kind of customer debt to AI. Financing receivables are what customers owe Dell when it lets them pay over time. On the July-quarter call, he said the growth in financing receivables "is effectively driven by the growth in the overall business, and it's anchored obviously in the expansion of AI".

title: Can D-Wave Stock Outlast Its $143 Million Cash Burn?

Today's big story: Reported SEC Probe: Could Nvidia Stock Fall To $92?

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) stock has fallen 72.2% over the past year, while the S&P 500 gained 5.3%. And the company still spends far more than it brings in. On its November 10, 2026 call, management said third-quarter operating expenses rose 84% from a year earlier. The quarter's loss per share also came in a little wider than the consensus estimate. So how fast is D-Wave going through its cash? At the third quarter's pace, its net cash would last about ten quarters.

D-Wave Is Burning Cash Faster Than A Year Ago

D-Wave spent $143 million more than it took in over the twelve months to September 30, 2026, a negative free cash flow. A year earlier, that gap was $55.1 million. Sales fell at the same time. Revenue dropped to $13.2 million from $24.1 million over the same periods.

D-Wave Quantum's cash outflow rose to $143 million over the past year, from $55.1 million a year earlier. If this stock is a big part of your savings, you are counting on D-Wave's cash lasting as long as you hold. Instead of one company, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio owns 30 quality companies in equal amounts, and it is up more than 105% since September 2020. Look inside HQ.

The cash balance fell further than the spending alone would explain. Management said cash and marketable securities fell 40% over the year, to $503.4 million. It put that mainly down to the $253 million D-Wave paid for Quantum Circuits in January 2026. So the cash outflow has grown, but the deal took the biggest bite out of the cash.

At Today's Pace, D-Wave Has Years Of Cash

At the past year's pace, D-Wave's net cash would cover about three years of cash outflow. On September 30, 2026, the company held $446 million more in cash and short-term investments than it owed in debt. If the third quarter's outflow of $43.3 million simply repeated, that net cash would last about ten quarters.

Owning the stock through a long wait has meant sitting through steep falls. D-Wave stock fell 73% from peak to low in the summer-fall 2023 yield shock, against a 9.5% fall for the S&P 500.

What Could Stretch D-Wave's Cash Further

D-Wave has funding and sales lined up that its reported revenue and cash do not yet show. In the third quarter, it signed an agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $100 million of CHIPS and Science Act funding. That money depends on D-Wave meeting set milestones. Bookings for the first nine months of 2026 reached $37.4 million, up 611% from a year earlier. They include a $20 million system sale to Florida Atlantic University. Management expects to recognize a large part of that revenue on delivery in the fourth quarter.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Twenty years ago, Dell was a PC company. It sold desktops and notebooks straight to buyers, each built to order. Today most of its sales come from servers, storage and networking. How did it get here?

On Friday, Nov 20, AI stocks sold off. Dell fell 11.0%, Nvidia 14.0% and the S&P 500 fund (SPY) 3.6%. Stock returns below are at that close.

Dell's fiscal years end in late January or early February. In fiscal 2006, Dell sold $55.8 billion. It kept 6.5 cents of each dollar of sales as profit. Its rival HP sold $91.7 billion that year. In 2007, Michael Dell came back as CEO.

In its latest quarter, Dell's sales were $47.0 billion, up 58% from a year earlier. Servers, storage and networking brought in $31.8 billion, about two-thirds. PCs and other devices brought in $15.0 billion.

Over the last 12 months, Dell sold $151.2 billion. That is 2.7 times its 2006 sales. Over five years, Dell stock returned 447%, against 58% for the S&P 500.

Dell's server sales ride on the same AI spending as Nvidia and Broadcom. If you live off what you have saved, you may not want all of it tied to that one boom. Michael Dell has written that going private with Silver Lake freed Dell from Wall Street's quarterly demands. Buying EMC added storage for big companies. It also brought a stake in VMware. Dell later spun off VMware and used a VMware dividend to pay down debt. The deal years cost money. Dell had operating losses from fiscal 2015 through fiscal 2019.

Each step brought a different main buyer. First it was households, then corporate IT departments. Now it is AI cloud companies that order Nvidia-powered servers by the rack.

The mix of sales shows it. In fiscal 2019, PCs outsold the data-center unit, which sells servers, storage and networking. PCs brought in $43.2 billion, the data-center unit $36.7 billion. In fiscal 2026, the year to January 2026, the data-center unit passed PCs, $60.8 billion to $51.0 billion. In the first half of this fiscal year, it sold twice as much as PCs, $60.8 billion to $29.6 billion.

International Business Machines (IBM) is back in the headlines after IBM and Red Hat opened up wider access to their Lightwell Network security offering through Microsoft's cloud marketplace, putting open source software supply chain risk in sharper focus for investors.

For International Business Machines, the headlines have not translated into short term gains. The 7 day share price return is down 9.18% and the 30 day share price return is down 10.75%. However, the 3 year total shareholder return of 57.95% and 5 year total shareholder return of 133.17% point to momentum that has built over a longer horizon.

International Business Machines is coming off a sharp pullback after a long winning streak, which puts a simple tension in front of you. Has the bulk of the rerating already happened, or does the current price still leave meaningful upside on the table once valuation is stacked against IBM's cash flows and peers?

Most Popular Narrative: 12% Undervalued

International Business Machines closed at $224.44 while the most followed narrative on Simply Wall St pegs fair value at $256.08, so the narrative implies meaningful upside when that estimate is discounted at 9.55%.

According to kapirey, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the narrative, the long term thesis rests on IBM's shift toward hybrid cloud and AI as a software led platform business with strong cash generation and a broad enterprise footprint.

IBM represents a defensive growth technology investment transitioning into a software and AI led enterprise platform company. While topline growth remains moderate, improving mix (software), strong margins, and durable cash flows underpin a compelling long term investment case, particularly for investors seeking exposure to enterprise AI with lower volatility than pure play SaaS peers.
